subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.activity_title: From a Dot to an Endless Path

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.4 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: Name the line segments in Fig. 2.4 (points L, M, P, Q, R); identify which of the five marked points lie on exactly one segment and which lie on two segments.

time_bands.activity: Students press the tip of a sharpened pencil on paper to model a point, then press and drag to model a line segment. Teacher asks: what is the difference between the dot and the path? Students describe in their own words what a point is — a precise location with no length or breadth — and what a line segment is — the shortest path between two endpoints, named by those endpoints.

Students fold a sheet of paper once and open it to see the crease. Teacher asks: where does the crease start and where does it end? Students recognise the crease as a line segment AB or BA. Teacher then asks: what would happen if the crease never stopped? Students articulate that a line extends endlessly in both directions and can be named by any two points on it or by a lowercase letter.

Students examine several sets of two dots on their page and draw the unique line segment joining each pair. Teacher guides the observation: can you draw more than one straight path between the same two points? Students state that any two points determine exactly one line segment and, extending that idea, exactly one line through them.

Figure it Out Q2, section 2.4 p.16 (“Name the line segments in Fig. 2.4 (points L, M, P, Q, R); identify which points lie on one or two segments….”) — students work individually, then compare answers with a neighbour to check notation and reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that a point has no dimension and a line segment is the shortest connection between two endpoints, watch for students who confuse the notation AB (segment) with the idea of a full line through A and B — the crease analogy helps clarify boundaries. Students sometimes write segment names without both letters; reinforce the two-endpoint convention consistently.

periods.activity_title: One End Fixed, One End Free

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5 (T, A, N, B) and determine whether T is the starting point of each ray.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 2.4 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: From Fig. 2.6 name: (a) five points; (b) a line; (c) four rays; (d) five line segments.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 2.4 p.17
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ray OA starts at O and passes through A and B. (a) Can it also be named OB? Why? (b) Can OA be written as AO? Why or why not?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.4 p.16
homework.description: Draw rough figures and label appropriately for four geometric statements: (a) OP and OQ meet at O; (b) XY and PQ intersect at M; (c) line l contains E and F but not D; (d) point P lies on AB.

time_bands.activity: Teacher uses a torch beam as a physical model: the torch body is fixed (initial point), the beam travels endlessly in one direction. Students brainstorm other real-life examples — sun rays, searchlight — and articulate what distinguishes a ray from a line segment (one endpoint) and from a line (one endpoint, not two).

Students mark a point O on paper, draw several rays starting at O through labelled points P, Q, R. They name each ray using the starting point first — and discuss: does changing the order of letters change which ray is named? This leads to the rule that the initial point is always written first in the ray's name.

Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4 p.16 (“Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5 (T, A, N, B) and determine whether T is the starting point….”) — students work through the figure, then discuss with a partner. Figure it Out Q5, section 2.4 p.16 (“From Fig. 2.6 name five points, a line, four rays, five line segments….”) — students list all objects.

Figure it Out Q6, section 2.4 p.17 (“Ray OA starts at O and passes through A and B. Can it also be named OB? Can OA be written as AO?….”) — class discussion, with teacher gathering reasoning before confirming. Teacher closes by contrasting the notation rules for lines, segments, and rays.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on students’ understanding of line segments as bounded paths, the key insight here is that a ray is bounded on exactly one side. A frequent error is writing the initial point second — reinforce: ray name = initial point first, then any point on it. The torch-beam image is a strong anchor for the one-direction infinity.
materials: torch or flashlight (or a phone flashlight)

periods.activity_title: Two Rays Meet: Naming the Opening

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find angles in given pictures (bicycle, tiled pattern, ladder, bridge truss); draw the rays forming one angle and name its vertex.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.5 p.20
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain why ∠APB (where three rays from P are shown) cannot be labelled as ∠P.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.5 p.20
textbook_items_in_class.description: Name the angles marked in the given figure (rays from T through P, R, Q).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 2.5 p.20
homework.description: Mark three non-collinear points A, B, C; draw all lines through pairs; count and name the lines; name and mark all angles using A, B, C.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens a pair of scissors slightly and asks: what geometric object do you see at the pivot? Students respond and teacher formalises: an angle is two rays sharing a common starting point, that point being the vertex. Teacher introduces the notation ∠DBE — vertex is always the middle letter.

Students look at real-life images — compass, spectacles, hinged door — and identify the two arms and the vertex in each. Teacher emphasises that the size of an angle is the amount of rotation needed to move one arm onto the other, not the length of the arms.

Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5 p.19 (“Find angles in given pictures — bicycle, tiled pattern, ladder, bridge truss; draw the rays forming one angle and name its vertex….”) — students sketch the rays and label vertex. Then Figure it Out Q3, section 2.5 p.20 (“Explain why ∠APB cannot be labelled as ∠P….”) — brief pair discussion before class share.

Figure it Out Q4, section 2.5 p.20 (“Name the angles marked in the given figure — rays from T through P, R, Q….”) — students name each angle carefully using the three-letter convention, then teacher checks that vertex always occupies the middle position.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error at this stage is labelling an angle with only the vertex letter when multiple angles share that vertex — Q3’s question directly addresses this. Draw attention to the fact that the angle’s size depends on the opening (rotation) between the arms, not on how long the arms are drawn; this prepares students well for the comparison work ahead.

periods.activity_title: Which Opening Is Wider? Superimpose and Decide

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.6 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fold a rectangular sheet to create angles; name and compare angles formed between the fold and the sides; make different angles by varied folding and identify the largest and smallest.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.6 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which angle is greater in each case using the given figure (rays A, X, Y from O with B and C on base): (a) ∠AOB or ∠XOY; (b) ∠AOB or ∠XOB; (c) ∠XOB or ∠XOC. Discuss reasoning with friends.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.6 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which angle is greater: ∠XOY or ∠AOB (Fig. where arms of both angles are drawn from O)? Give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws two angles of evidently different sizes on the board and asks: how do you know which is larger? Students suggest eye estimates; teacher asks for a method that does not rely on guessing. The superimposition method is introduced: align vertices, align one arm, check whether the other arm of one angle falls inside, on, or outside the other.

Figure it Out Q1, section 2.6 p.23 (“Fold a rectangular sheet to create angles; compare angles formed; identify largest and smallest….”) — students fold paper to produce angles, physically superimpose by holding sheets up to light, and order their angles. Teacher then presents the transparent-circle method as an alternative: mark arc intercepts on a transparent sheet and compare without direct overlap.

Figure it Out Q2, section 2.6 p.23 (“Determine which angle is greater — ∠AOB or ∠XOY; ∠AOB or ∠XOB; ∠XOB or ∠XOC….”) — students reason from the figure and justify each comparison in a sentence, using the language of superimposition.

Figure it Out Q3, section 2.6 p.23 (“Which angle is greater: ∠XOY or ∠AOB? Give reasons….”) — students write a brief justification. Teacher uses this to state the equality criterion: two angles are equal when, upon superimposition, both arms and the vertex coincide exactly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conclude that a larger-looking diagram of an angle means a larger angle — arm length is irrelevant and superimposition reveals this. Watch for students who superimpose without aligning both the vertex and one arm, leading to incorrect comparisons. The equality criterion (all three elements coincide) is the deductive anchor for the rest of the section.
materials: rectangular sheets of paper (one per student)

periods.activity_title: Build, Order, and Challenge: Rotating Arms

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 1, p.25
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students make ‘rotating arms’ using two paper straws inserted into the arms of a paper clip, create several rotating arms with different angles, arrange them from smallest to largest by superimposition, then perform the slit-passing challenge — tracing one rotating arm onto cardboard to make an angle-shaped slit and identifying which shuffled arm passes through it.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes two paper straws and a paper clip to each student and demonstrates how to insert the straws into the two arms of the clip to create a rotating-arm model. Students make their own model and adjust the opening to several different angles.

Activity 1, p.25 (“Students make ‘rotating arms’, create several with different angles, arrange from smallest to largest by superimposition….”) — students create at least four models with visibly different openings, then work in groups of four to arrange all models in order from smallest to largest, justifying each placement by superimposition.

Slit-passing challenge from Activity 1, p.25: one student traces a chosen rotating arm onto cardboard and cuts the angle-shaped slit. The remaining models are shuffled and each student predicts which model’s angle will pass through the slit. Students test by sliding each arm through and record outcomes, discovering that arm length does not affect whether an angle passes — only the opening size matters.

Class debrief: teacher asks students to state in their own words what the slit challenge proved. Students articulate that angle size is determined by the rotation between arms, independent of arm length, connecting back to the definition of angle introduced earlier in the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The slit challenge is the conceptual payoff of this unit: if a model with longer arms but a smaller opening is predicted to pass through a slit cut for a model with shorter arms but a larger opening, students typically expect the longer arms to fail — this prediction error generates productive surprise. Ensure cardboard slits are cut cleanly so the test is conclusive. Circulate during ordering to check that superimposition (not visual estimation) is the method students use.

periods.activity_title: Straight, Right, Acute, Obtuse: A Paper-Fold Discovery

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.29
textbook_items_in_class.description: Count right angles in classroom windows and identify other right angles in the classroom.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.8 p.30
textbook_items_in_class.description: On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a straight angle in all different ways.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.31
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in the previous figures shown in the chapter.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.8 p.31
homework.description: Make a few acute angles and a few obtuse angles; draw them in different orientations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher narrates Vidya’s notebook scenario: a notebook lying flat has two arms of the angle pointing in exactly opposite directions, forming a straight angle. Students fold a sheet of paper so that one straight edge folds onto itself, producing a crease — the two halves of the edge now form a straight angle of 180°.

Students fold the straight edge in half again, bringing the two arms of the straight angle together — the crease now bisects the straight angle. Teacher asks: how many equal angles did we get? Students observe two equal angles and the teacher introduces the right angle (90°) and the term perpendicular for lines meeting at a right angle.

Teacher defines acute (less than a right angle) and obtuse (greater than a right angle, less than a straight angle) using examples from the chapter figures. Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.29 (“Count right angles in classroom windows and identify other right angles….”) — students survey the room and list. Figure it Out Q2, section 2.8 p.30 (“On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a straight angle in all different ways….”) — students draw several configurations.

Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.31 (“Identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in the previous figures shown in the chapter….”) — students classify angles from earlier drawings, labelling each type. Teacher circulates, checking that students distinguish obtuse from straight angles correctly.

periods.teacher_notes: The paper-folding sequence (flat edge → straight angle → fold in half → right angle) makes the relationship between 180° and 90° tangible before numbers are introduced. A common confusion is treating any wide angle as obtuse — reinforce that an obtuse angle must be strictly less than a straight angle. Figure it Out Q3 p.31 (explaining the etymology of acute and obtuse) is a good self-study enrichment pointer for curious students.

periods.activity_title: Why Right Angles Are Equal: Reasoning Through Folds

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.30
textbook_items_in_class.description: On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a right angle in all different ways (using the hint that line CAB must be bisected).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.31
textbook_items_in_class.description: Get a slanting crease on paper; fold to get a perpendicular crease. (a) How many right angles result? Justify they are exact right angles. (b) Describe the folding procedure so another person can replicate it.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.31
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain why the words ‘acute’ (sharp) and ‘obtuse’ (blunt) have been chosen for these angle types.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.32
textbook_items_in_class.description: Count the number of acute angles in each of the three given triangle figures; predict the next figure and its acute angle count; identify the numerical pattern.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the reasoning question: we folded a straight angle in half and called the result a right angle — but how do we know both halves are exactly equal? Students discuss in pairs; teacher formalises that superimposition of the two halves (aligning the crease) shows the two angles coincide exactly, establishing that bisecting a straight angle always yields two right angles.

Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.30 (“On a dot grid, get a right angle in all different ways — line CAB must be bisected….”) — students apply the bisection reasoning to construct right angles on the grid, justifying each by naming the straight angle they bisected. Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.31 (“Get a slanting crease; fold to get a perpendicular crease; justify they are exact right angles….”) — students perform the fold and write a brief justification.

Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.31 (“Explain why ‘acute’ (sharp) and ‘obtuse’ (blunt) have been chosen….”) — students write a sentence connecting the visual sharpness of an acute angle to its name, then share aloud. This exercise anchors vocabulary to visual and etymological reasoning.

Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.32 (“Count acute angles in each triangle figure; predict the next figure and its count; identify the pattern….”) — students count, predict, and state the numerical pattern in words. Teacher uses this as an example of inductive pattern recognition within a deductive framework.

periods.teacher_notes: The central reasoning move here is using superimposition to prove equality — the same tool used for comparing arbitrary angles now proves that two right angles produced by bisecting a straight angle are necessarily equal. Watch for students who accept the result without justification; prompt them with “how do you know both halves are the same size?”. The pattern task in Q4 p.32 extends naturally for students who finish early.

periods.activity_title: 360 Equal Parts: Building a Measurement System

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.34
textbook_items_in_class.description: A circle divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12 equal parts is shown; write the degree measure of each resulting angle near the indicated sector.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.35
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the unlabelled protractor diagram, write the measures of ∠KAL, ∠WAL, and ∠TAK by counting 1° units (and in groups of 5° or 10° using medium and large marks).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Think!, section 2.9 p.40
textbook_items_in_class.description: In Fig. 2.19, explain why ∠AOB = ∠BOC = ∠COD = ∠DOE = ∠EOF = ∠FOG = ∠GOH = ∠HOI (fill in the common value and justify).

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the historical note: the full-turn is divided into 360 equal parts because 360 is highly divisible — by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 and more — tracing this choice to Babylonian calendars and the Rigveda’s wheel of 360 spokes. Students reason from this: a half-turn (straight angle) = 180°, a quarter-turn (right angle) = 90°, connecting the degree system to what they already know from the paper-folding work.

Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.34 (“A circle divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12 equal parts; write the degree measure of each resulting angle….”) — students calculate by dividing 360° by the number of equal parts, reinforcing the 360-unit system inductively.

Teacher introduces the unlabelled protractor figure and explains its dual scale. Students count 1° marks in groups of 5° and 10° using the medium and large marks. Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.35 (“Using the unlabelled protractor diagram, write the measures of ∠KAL, ∠WAL, and ∠TAK by counting 1° units….”) — students read three angles and reason about which scale to use for each.

Think!, section 2.9 p.40 (“Explain why ∠AOB = ∠BOC = ∠COD = … = ∠HOI; fill in the common value and justify….”) — students reason that if the full 360° is divided equally among the eight sub-angles, each must be 45°, and write a justification sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: The connection between the historical divisibility argument and the derived values for straight and right angles is the conceptual core here — ensure students state it in their own words rather than copying. A common error is reading from the wrong scale on the dual protractor; encourage students to check their answer with an estimate (acute angle must be less than 90°, etc.) before recording.
materials: printed or projected unlabelled protractor diagram

periods.activity_title: Reading, Folding, and Making Your Own Protractor

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.36
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the labelled protractor figure (rays O, P, Q, R, S, T, U), name all different angles and write their degree measures; determine which scale (inner or outer) to use and apply subtraction where needed.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 2, p.37
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students make their own protractor by successive paper folding: cut a circle, fold to semicircle (180°), fold again to quarter-circle (90°), fold again to mark 45° and 135°, fold once more to mark 22.5° and 67.5° etc., then unfold and label all creases, identifying angle bisectors and reading off the resulting degree measures.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 2.9 p.41
textbook_items_in_class.description: Measure and write the degree measures for six angles (a–f) drawn in varied orientations.

homework.description: Six protractor-reading figures (∠U, ∠V, ∠W, ∠X, ∠Y, ∠Z) show incorrect student usage; identify the error(s) in each and explain how the correct reading should be made.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.36 (“Using the labelled protractor figure — rays O, P, Q, R, S, T, U — name all different angles and write their degree measures; determine which scale to use, apply subtraction where needed….”) — students work through systematically, choosing inner or outer scale for each ray and using subtraction when an angle spans from a non-zero ray.

Activity 2, p.37 (“Make your own protractor: cut a circle, fold to semicircle (180°), fold to quarter-circle (90°), fold to mark 45° and 135°, fold once more to mark 22.5° and 67.5°, unfold and label all creases….”) — students fold step by step, label each crease with its degree value, and identify each crease as an angle bisector of the previous fold.

Figure it Out Q5, section 2.9 p.41 (“Measure and write the degree measures for six angles (a–f) drawn in varied orientations….”) — students use either the standard protractor or their handmade one to measure, checking that their two instruments agree on at least one angle and resolving any discrepancy by identifying alignment errors.

periods.teacher_notes: The handmade protractor links each degree value to a physical fold, making the bisector concept concrete — each crease halves the angle of the previous crease. Watch for students who do not align the protractor’s centre on the vertex, the most common measurement error. Mind the Mistake (p.44) sent home will surface the full range of misalignment errors and is worth discussing at the start of the next unit.
materials: circular paper pieces (one per student, cut before class)

periods.activity_title: Draw It, Guess It, Score It: Angle Drawing Games

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.10 p.50
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use a protractor to draw angles of 110°, 40°, 75°, 112°, and 134°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let’s Play a Game #1, section 2.10 p.48
textbook_items_in_class.description: Team game: one team secretly draws an angle with a protractor; the other team visually estimates the measure; score is the absolute difference in degrees. Each team gets five turns; lowest score wins.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let’s Play a Game #2, section 2.10 p.48
textbook_items_in_class.description: Team game: one team announces a degree measure; a player from the other team draws it freehand on the board (teammates guide verbally); score is the absolute difference between drawn and intended angle. Five turns each.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.10 p.50
homework.description: Draw an angle whose measure equals the given angle (∠HIJ); write the steps followed.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the four-step procedure for drawing a specified angle: draw a base ray from the vertex, place the protractor centre on the vertex, locate the correct degree mark on the appropriate scale, and join with a ruler. Students follow along to draw 30° (∠TIN) as the demonstration angle.

Figure it Out Q2, section 2.10 p.50 (“Use a protractor to draw angles of 110°, 40°, 75°, 112°, and 134°….”) — students draw each angle independently, labelling the vertex and both arms. Teacher circulates to check that the inner vs. outer scale is chosen correctly for each measure.

Let’s Play a Game #1, section 2.10 p.48 (“One team secretly draws an angle with a protractor; the other team visually estimates; score is absolute difference in degrees; five turns each….”) — class splits into two teams. Scores are tracked on the board; the emphasis is on developing visual angle sense.

Let’s Play a Game #2, section 2.10 p.48 (“One team announces a degree measure; a player draws it freehand while teammates guide verbally; score is absolute difference; five turns each….”) — teams compete. At the end, teacher draws attention to what types of angles were hardest to estimate and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The games build angle-sense that pure procedural drawing cannot — students begin to feel what 75° or 110° looks like. Watch for students who draw a base ray and then rotate the protractor around instead of keeping its centre fixed on the vertex. The homework (Figure it Out Q3 p.50) asks students to copy a given angle using the four steps in writing, consolidating procedural fluency.
materials: chalk or whiteboard marker for team game

textbook_segments.title: Types of Angles and their Measures

periods.activity_title: Classifying Every Angle: From Acute to Reflex

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.51
textbook_items_in_class.description: On dot grids, join A to other grid points to get (a) an acute angle, (b) an obtuse angle, (c) a reflex angle; mark the intended angles with curves.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.11 p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use a protractor to find the measures of ∠PTR, ∠PTQ, ∠PTW, and ∠WTP from the given figure; classify each as acute, obtuse, right, or reflex.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.11 p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate the size of each of six given angles (a–f) and then measure with a protractor; classify each as acute, right, obtuse, or reflex.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the complete five-type classification as a reference chart on the board: acute (0°–90°), right (exactly 90°), obtuse (90°–180°), straight (exactly 180°), reflex (180°–360°). Students copy and add one drawn example of each in varied orientations.

Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.51 (“On dot grids, join A to other grid points to get an acute angle, an obtuse angle, a reflex angle; mark with curves….”) — students construct each type on the grid and mark the angle with a curve on the correct (intended) side, practising the convention of indicating which opening is meant.

Figure it Out Q2, section 2.11 p.52 (“Use a protractor to find the measures of ∠PTR, ∠PTQ, ∠PTW, and ∠WTP; classify each….”) — students measure, record, and classify. Teacher asks: how do you measure a reflex angle? Students suggest measuring the non-reflex partner and subtracting from 360°.

Figure it Out Q2, section 2.11 p.53 (“Estimate the size of each of six given angles (a–f) and then measure; classify each as acute, right, obtuse, or reflex….”) — students estimate before measuring, recording both estimate and actual, and reflecting on how close their estimates were.

periods.teacher_notes: The reflex angle is new in this section and students often miss it by defaulting to the smaller of the two possible openings — reinforce that the curve marking explicitly shows which angle is intended. A useful self-study pointer: Figure it Out Q3 p.31 (from section 2.8) asked about the etymology of acute and obtuse; connecting that to the new labels at this stage deepens vocabulary retention.

textbook_segments.title: Types of Angles and their Measures

periods.activity_title: Angles in Letters, Chakra, and Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let’s Explore, section 2.11 p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given ∠TER = 80° in a figure where ∠REB is a straight angle and ∠SET is perpendicular context, find the measures of ∠BET and ∠SET.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 2.11 p.54
textbook_items_in_class.description: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes. Find the angle between two adjacent spokes; find the largest acute angle formed between two spokes.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 2.11 p.54
textbook_items_in_class.description: Puzzle: find all acute angle measures such that double, triple, and quadruple the measure are still acute, but five times the measure is obtuse.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.11 p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw the letter ‘M’ such that the angles on the sides are 40° each and the angle in the middle is 60°.

time_bands.activity: Let’s Explore, section 2.11 p.53 (“Given ∠TER = 80° where ∠REB is a straight angle and ∠SET is in a perpendicular context, find ∠BET and ∠SET….”) — students use the straight angle (180°) and right angle (90°) properties established through paper folding to derive the unknown measures, writing a step-by-step solution.

Figure it Out Q6, section 2.11 p.54 (“The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes; find the angle between two adjacent spokes; find the largest acute angle between two spokes….”) — students divide 360° by 24, then explore multiples of the unit angle to find which is still acute.

Figure it Out Q7, section 2.11 p.54 (“Find all acute angle measures such that double, triple, quadruple are still acute but five times is obtuse….”) — students set up inequalities in words (the angle must be less than 90° ÷ 4 = 22.5°, and five times it must exceed 90°) and identify the valid range, listing examples.

Figure it Out Q4, section 2.11 p.53 (“Draw the letter ‘M’ such that the angles on the sides are 40° each and the angle in the middle is 60°….”) — students construct the letter using a protractor, reinforcing drawing accuracy. Teacher closes by having two or three students display their letters and comparing angle accuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: The Ashoka Chakra problem and the multiplier puzzle both require applying the full classification system — students must know all five boundaries to reason correctly. Watch for students who write 360 ÷ 24 = 16° but then cannot name the largest acute angle between non-adjacent spokes (successive multiples of 15° up to 75°). The letter-drawing task consolidates procedural accuracy in a creative context.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes a point in geometry?

options.label: A
options.text: A dot that has a small but measurable width

options.label: B
options.text: A flat surface that extends in all directions

options.label: C
options.text: A precise location with no length, breadth, or height

options.label: D
options.text: A short path between two locations

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A precise location with no length, breadth, or height.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition of a point as a location with zero dimensions.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses a point with a line segment, which is a path between two endpoints.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses a point with a plane, which is a flat surface extending in two dimensions.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks a dot drawn on paper literally is the point, confusing the physical model with the geometric abstraction.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the compass-tip and pencil-point examples in the chapter to anchor the definition.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give one more real-life model of a point in their own words and explain why it fits.

items.prompt: Ray PQ starts at P and passes through Q. Which of the following statements about this ray is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It can also be named QP because the two endpoints are interchangeable

options.label: B
options.text: It extends endlessly in both directions from P and Q

options.label: C
options.text: It has a fixed starting point P and extends endlessly through Q in one direction

options.label: D
options.text: It is the same as line segment PQ because both involve P and Q

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A ray has a fixed starting point (P) and extends endlessly through the other named point (Q) in one direction only.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition of a ray: one fixed initial point, endless extension in one direction.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not understand that the order of letters in a ray name is fixed — the initial point must come first.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses a ray (one-ended) with a line (two-ended, extending in both directions).
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses a ray with a line segment, which has two endpoints and finite length.

inclusivity.support: Refer the student back to the torch-beam example to recall the one-direction, one-endpoint nature of a ray.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words how a ray differs from both a line segment and a line.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4 p.16
exercise.description: Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5 (T, A, N, B) and determine whether T is the starting point of each ray.

items.prompt: Three rays PA, PB, and PC all start at the same point P. A student labels the angle between PA and PC as ∠P. Why is this labelling incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: An angle cannot be formed by rays that share a starting point

options.label: B
options.text: The angle must be named using the lengths of the arms, not letters

options.label: C
options.text: The label ∠P is ambiguous because there are multiple angles at vertex P

options.label: D
options.text: The vertex of an angle must always be the last letter, not the middle letter

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Using only ∠P is ambiguous when several angles share vertex P; the angle must be named with three letters, with the vertex as the middle letter, to identify which specific angle is meant.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the three-letter naming convention: one letter from each arm, vertex in the middle.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has the position of the vertex letter inverted — the vertex is always the middle letter, not the last.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student misunderstands the definition of an angle; angles are precisely formed by two rays sharing a starting point.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses naming conventions with measurement; angles are named with point labels, not arm lengths.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the scissors example in the chapter to recall how the pivot is the vertex and both blades are the arms.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to draw a figure with four rays from one point and name every distinct angle that can be formed.

exercise.description: Find angles in given pictures (bicycle, tiled pattern, ladder, bridge truss); draw the rays forming one angle and name its vertex.

items.prompt: A straight angle is formed when two arms of an angle point in exactly opposite directions. What is the measure of a straight angle, and how many right angles does it contain?

options.label: A
options.text: 90°, containing one right angle

options.label: B
options.text: 180°, containing two right angles

options.label: C
options.text: 180°, containing three right angles

options.label: D
options.text: 360°, containing four right angles

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A straight angle measures 180° and contains exactly two right angles (each 90°), as shown by bisecting the straight angle through paper folding.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall that bisecting a straight angle (180°) yields two equal right angles (90° each).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses a straight angle with a right angle, recalling only the 90° value.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses a straight angle with a full turn (360°), which contains four right angles.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly recalls 180° but miscounts the right angles; three right angles would total 270°.

inclusivity.support: Refer the student to the paper-folding demonstration where a flat edge was folded in half to produce two equal right-angle creases.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why bisecting a straight angle must always yield two equal angles.

items.section_title: Types of Angles and their Measures
items.prompt: An angle measures 215°. Which type of angle is this?

options.label: A
options.text: Obtuse

options.label: B
options.text: Reflex

options.label: C
options.text: Right

options.label: D
options.text: Straight

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 215° is a reflex angle because it lies between 180° and 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the classification: reflex angles measure strictly between 180° and 360°.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student knows obtuse angles are wide but does not have the 180° upper boundary in mind, placing 215° in the obtuse category.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates 215° as 'close to' a straight angle (180°) but does not distinguish the exact boundary.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student recalls right angle as a special angle type but does not connect it to the specific measure of 90°.

inclusivity.support: Let the student consult the five-type classification chart (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex) and locate 215° on it.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to name the non-reflex partner of this angle and state what the two angles sum to.

items.section_title: Types of Angles and their Measures
items.prompt: In a figure, ∠REB = 180° (a straight angle) and ∠TER = 80°. Without using a protractor, state the measure of ∠BET and explain how you found it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠BET = 100°. Since ∠REB is a straight angle (180°) and ray ET lies between rays ER and EB, ∠BET = 180° − ∠TER = 180° − 80° = 100°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the property that angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

inclusivity.support: Draw the straight angle and mark the two sub-angles to help the student see that they must add to 180°.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if ∠SET is a right angle (90°) and ∠TER = 80°, what is ∠SER? Justify with the same method.

exercise.description: Given ∠TER = 80° in a figure where ∠REB is a straight angle and ∠SET is perpendicular context, find the measures of ∠BET and ∠SET.

items.prompt: Two angles ∠PQR and ∠XYZ are drawn on separate sheets of paper. A student places one sheet over the other, aligns the vertices Q and Y, and aligns one pair of arms. The free arm of ∠PQR falls inside ∠XYZ. What does this tell you about the sizes of the two angles? Justify your answer using the superimposition method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠PQR is smaller than ∠XYZ. When vertices are aligned and one arm of each angle coincides, the free arm of the smaller angle lies inside the larger angle — meaning less rotation is needed to reach it. Since the free arm of ∠PQR falls inside ∠XYZ, ∠PQR requires less rotation and is therefore the smaller angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the superimposition method: align vertices and one arm; the angle whose free arm falls inside the other is the smaller angle.

inclusivity.support: Pair the student with a partner to physically fold and overlap two paper angles, talking through the alignment steps before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what would you observe if the two angles were equal? Describe what superimposition would look like in that case.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.6 p.23
exercise.description: Fold a rectangular sheet to create angles; name and compare angles formed between the fold and the sides; make different angles by varied folding and identify the largest and smallest.

items.prompt: A student folds a sheet of paper so that one straight edge folds exactly onto itself, producing a crease. The student then folds the paper again so that the two halves of the straight edge coincide. Using the idea of superimposition, explain why the two angles created by the second fold must be exactly equal, and state what special name each of these angles is given.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The first fold creates a straight angle of 180° — the two halves of the straight edge are the two arms of this angle. The second fold brings these two arms together; because the fold is a bisection, the two resulting angles are mirror images of each other. When one is placed on the other (superimposed), the vertices coincide and both arms align exactly — this means the two angles are equal. Each is half of 180°, so each measures 90°. An angle of exactly 90° is called a right angle. Two lines that meet at a right angle are called perpendicular.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the bisection argument: the second fold is a superimposition in itself — both halves of the straight angle coincide exactly, proving equality at 90° each.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to physically perform the two folds and describe in speech what they see before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the premise: if instead of folding a straight angle in half you fold a right angle in half, what angle would each portion be? Justify using the same reasoning.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.30
exercise.description: On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a right angle in all different ways (using the hint that line CAB must be bisected).

items.prompt: A full turn is divided into 360 equal parts, each called one degree. A circle is divided into 6 equal sectors. Without measuring, explain why each sector angle must be 60°, and state what type of angle this is.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A full turn = 360°. Dividing equally into 6 parts gives 360° ÷ 6 = 60° per sector. Since 60° is less than 90° (a right angle), each sector angle is an acute angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the full 360° by the number of equal parts; compare the result to 90° to classify.

inclusivity.support: Refer the student to the circle-division table from the chapter (Figure it Out, p.34) as a visual anchor for the division.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the circle were divided so that each sector angle is exactly 45°, how many equal sectors would there be? Justify.

exercise.description: A circle divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12 equal parts is shown; write the degree measure of each resulting angle near the indicated sector.

items.prompt: Arun makes three rotating-arm models. Model P has short arms and a wide opening. Model Q has long arms and a narrow opening. Model R has medium arms and the same opening as Model P. Arun cuts an angle-shaped slit by tracing Model Q. Which models will pass through the slit: P, Q, R, or none? Explain your answer using the relationship between arm length and angle size.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Only Model Q will pass through the slit. The slit is cut to match the opening (angle size) of Model Q — narrow. Model P and Model R both have a wider opening than Model Q, so they will not fit through the slit. Arm length does not matter; only the size of the angle (the amount of opening) determines whether a model passes through.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the principle that angle size depends on the opening (rotation), not on arm length; only the model whose opening matches the slit passes through.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the three models as open V-shapes with different widths and use the sketch to compare openings visually.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if Model R has the same opening as Model P but longer arms, would Model R’s arms stick out of the slit even if the angle itself cannot pass? Explain what part of the model interacts with the slit.

exercise.description: Students make ‘rotating arms’ using two paper straws inserted into the arms of a paper clip, create several rotating arms with different angles, arrange them from smallest to largest by superimposition, then perform the slit-passing challenge.

items.prompt: A protractor is placed with its centre on vertex X. Ray XA reads 0° on the outer scale. Ray XB reads 55° on the outer scale. Ray XC reads 130° on the outer scale. Find: (a) the measure of ∠AXB, (b) the measure of ∠AXC, and (c) the measure of ∠BXC. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) ∠AXB = 55° − 0° = 55°. (b) ∠AXC = 130° − 0° = 130°. (c) ∠BXC = 130° − 55° = 75°. All three are found by subtracting the two scale readings that form each angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the protractor scale at each ray and subtract the two readings to find the angle between any pair of rays.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line from 0° to 130° with marks at 55° and 130° to help the student visualise the subtraction.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if ray XD reads 200° on a full-circle scale, what is the reflex angle ∠AXD, and how would you use a standard semicircular protractor to verify it?

exercise.description: Using the labelled protractor figure (rays O, P, Q, R, S, T, U), name all different angles and write their degree measures; determine which scale (inner or outer) to use and apply subtraction where needed.

items.prompt: Draw an angle of 75° at vertex M, labelling it ∠AMB. Then, without lifting your protractor, draw a second angle of 110° at the same vertex M, sharing arm MA, and label it ∠AMC. Calculate the measure of ∠BMC and state whether it is acute, obtuse, or reflex. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Draw base ray MA. Step 2: Align protractor centre on M, locate 75° and draw ray MB — ∠AMB = 75°. Step 3: Locate 110° on the same scale from MA and draw ray MC — ∠AMC = 110°. Step 4: ∠BMC = ∠AMC − ∠AMB = 110° − 75° = 35°. Since 35° < 90°, ∠BMC is an acute angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw each angle from the same base ray using the four-step protractor procedure; find the angle between the two new rays by subtraction.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first draw each angle on a separate diagram with a ruler guide before combining them at vertex M.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if a third ray MD is drawn at 160° from MA, what are the measures of ∠CMD and ∠BMD, and how would you classify each?
